blocks.heading: Elul, the days of favor and the second luchos

paragraphs.text: The Rav opens with the forty days of favor, when Moshe went up for the second luchos and the people waited, broken after the sin of the egel. The teshuvah they did then, he says, left a mark on these days for all generations. Chazal say Moshe left no corner of heaven untouched, repairing the root of every Jewish soul. And the second luchos, given to baalei teshuvah, were greater than the first.

Turning to the parsha of shmitah, 'at the end of seven years', the Rav explains that the word shmitah means letting go, and the Torah calls it 'shmitah to Hashem'. A Midrash teaches that what a person does in this world, Hashem does in heaven; this is why He gave mitzvos, each one an act that brings about its counterpart above.

A Midrash says every seventh is beloved: Shabbos among the days and Tishrei among the months. Sin, beginning with Adam's, creates a debt that must be paid. The Rav notes that the shmitah cycle of years is counted from Tishrei, every seventh being a time of forgiveness.

blocks.heading: Releasing others' debts before Rosh Hashanah

paragraphs.text: From here the Rav explains the mitzvah of releasing debts. Hashem wants to forgive us our debt, so He commanded that we release what others owe us; by letting go below we arouse the release above. This happens each Tishrei and every Shabbos, a small Rosh Hashanah.

He brings the Gemara that the Satan has power on every day of the year except Yom Kippur. In Elul, therefore, one is mochel others before Rosh Hashanah, as the Shulchan Aruch says. He adds that the davening of this time should begin by accepting the mitzvah of loving one's fellow as oneself.

Now, says the Rav, everyone must strengthen others in serving Hashem, and the great danger is letzanus, scoffing, which cools Yiddishkeit. Rabbi Tzadok writes in Tzidkas HaTzaddik that the root of all good is emunah, which is why the Ten Commandments open with 'I am Hashem your G-d'; emunah is the entrance to serving Hashem.
The root of all bad is letzanus, the opposite of emunah and the entrance to the other side. Just as one who comes to defile himself is given an opening, Heaven helps the scoffer in his scoffing.

Rabbi Tzadok adds that just as a person arouses Heaven with mitzvos, so with scoffing: Heaven supplies him with good jokes. A bochur who davens with warmth is mocked, and one joke can empty him out. This, the Rav says, is the kelipah of Amalek, whom the Midrash calls a scoffer.

The Gemara says scoffers do not receive the Shechinah. Rabbi Tzadok explains that a scoffer is not let into davening: each part of tefillah is a palace, and he is turned away, as guards were placed at Gan Eden after Adam sinned.

A person is where his thoughts are, as the Ba'al Shem Tov taught. The Besht once greeted a man after davening; he had been in Danzig with his merchandise. The scoffer loses all connection to davening and learning.
The Midrash applies to Pharaoh the passuk that calls the arrogant man a scoffer. The Rav says he searched the Chumash and the Midrash and found no joke of Pharaoh's. Why, then, is he called a letz?

He asks a further question. Pharaoh was warned and saw each plague arrive as Moshe foretold, yet withstood them with an almost superhuman strength. A logical man who lives by calculation would have given in after one plague or two, since it was ruining his country.
The answer is his letzanus. A joke is an escape, the opposite of reality. Plagues are suffering, but a joke takes a person away from his situation, so he never faces it and never submits to Moshe.

A scoffer never answers with logic. The Rav tells of a teacher who described to young students the good prepared for tzaddikim, the Leviasan among it; a child raised his hand and said he does not like fish, and the derashah was over. One scoffing remark pushes away a hundred rebukes; this, the Rav says, is the destruction.

What was Pharaoh's punishment? The Rav brings the passuk that a Jew should tell his children 'that I made sport of Egypt', and Rashi's explanation that Hashem mocked Egypt. Measure for measure: Hashem let Pharaoh make good jokes, then made a joke of him.
The Rav then describes how Yosef gathered the money of the whole world into Egypt, making it the richest land and the envy of its neighbors, until all that wealth went out with Yosef's family.

blocks.heading: Rosh Hashanah as a day of emes

paragraphs.text: Much of this part of the recording is lost. In what survives, the Rav calls this the preparation for Rosh Hashanah and asks what the seal of its brachah is: it speaks of emes, and Rosh Hashanah is emes, the opposite of scoffing's escape from reality.
Since the Torah obligates every Jew, the Rav says, each one must make a cheshbon for himself.

blocks.heading: Elul and Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael

paragraphs.text: The closing is poorly recorded. The Rav says that in Elul Moshe began bringing the luchos down from heaven, and a Jew must now bring his heart along, purify it and bind himself to Hashem. He cites 'one thing I ask of Hashem', to dwell in His house all the days of one's life.
He speaks of giving all the wealth of one's house out of love, the love between a Jew and Hashem. He ends with Hashem's great love for a Jew and wishes for a good Elul and a good Rosh Hashanah.
